title: #127. How the Leash Chokes the Spirit
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray shares the opening of Chapter 3 of his book Restoring Childhood, which argues that play and other independent activities are essential for healthy child development. The excerpt's rhetorical move is a thought experiment: readers are asked to imagine a spouse or friend controlling them the way parents now monitor children, and an employer controlling them the way teachers control students. Gray suggests that such treatment, especially when done out of love and for one's own good, would feel imprisoning and belittling and would turn unhappiness inward. He then insists that children are not as different from adults as many assume, needing privacy, trust, and growing amounts of unsupervised activity. The excerpt closes by previewing the chapter's evidence that independent activity, chores, and jobs are the primary means by which children learn to solve problems, regulate emotions, and face the future with confidence.
points: Gray's thought experiment reverses perspective, asking adults to imagine living under the surveillance and control routinely applied to children.
He argues that control exercised lovingly for someone's own good can be more damaging than hostile control, because it signals incompetence and turns unhappiness inward.
Children, he contends, need steadily increasing privacy, trust, and unsupervised activity as they grow, which is simply what growing up means.
The chapter frames independent play, home chores, and outside jobs as the main vehicles for building resilience and confidence about adulthood.
quotes: Imagine that your spouse or your closest friend had the same power over you that parents typically have over children. Now imagine that this person, out of their love and care for you, uses that power in ways analogous to the ways today's parents commonly try to protect and guide their kids.
You are reprimanded even if you are a minute late. You are not allowed to leave your seat while at work except at specified breaks.

The fact that all this is being done "for your own good" by people who love and care for you would likely make you feel even worse. You must be truly incompetent if all this is being done for your own good.

Yes, I know, children are not adults. But they are not as different from adults as many people seem to believe. Like all of us, children need some privacy, some trust, some opportunities for unsupervised independent activity.
Did you not need increasing amounts of independence and trust as you grew up, to feel happy, confident, and respected?
Through independent activities, kids learn they can solve problems, survive setbacks, make friends, regulate their fear and anger, and, generally, take charge of their own life.
